reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Catecholamine-secreting tumours arising from adrenal medulla (pheochromocytoma) or extra-adrenal sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia (paraganglioma)
The classic paroxysmal triad is episodic headache, palpitations, and sweating, often with hypertension that may be sustained or episodic
Should be suspected in resistant hypertension, hypertension in the young, hypertensive spikes during anaesthesia or procedures, and incidentally found adrenal masses
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating excess catecholamine metabolites, with plasma or urinary fractionated metanephrines being the most sensitive tests
Imaging localises the tumour after biochemical confirmation, and functional imaging helps detect extra-adrenal or metastatic disease

A substantial proportion are associated with hereditary syndromes such as MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, and SDH-related paraganglioma syndromes, so genetic evaluation is recommended
Definitive treatment is surgical resection, but adequate preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade before any beta-blockade is essential to prevent catastrophic intraoperative crises
Because malignancy cannot be reliably predicted histologically, lifelong biochemical and clinical surveillance is required
reference.pathophysiology: Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas are neuroendocrine tumours of chromaffin or paraganglionic tissue that synthesise, store, and episodically release catecholamines (noradrenaline, adrenaline, and sometimes dopamine). Unregulated catecholamine secretion produces alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and beta-mediated cardiac stimulation, causing paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, and end-organ stress. Chronic catecholamine excess can lead to cardiomyopathy and volume contraction. A large fraction harbour germline or somatic mutations in genes such as RET, VHL, NF1, and the succinate dehydrogenase (SDHx) complex, linking them to defined hereditary syndromes and influencing malignant potential and secretory phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Hypoglycaemia and other causes of adrenergic surges
Drug effects (sympathomimetics, monoamine oxidase interactions, withdrawal states)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma free or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines as first-line biochemical testing
CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis to localise adrenal or extra-adrenal tumours
Functional imaging such as MIBG or somatostatin-receptor/PET studies for metastatic or extra-adrenal disease
Genetic testing given the high rate of heritable disease
Assessment for associated syndromic features and screening of at-risk relatives
Cardiac evaluation for catecholamine cardiomyopathy where indicated
redFlags: Pheochromocytoma crisis with severe hypertension, arrhythmia, cardiovascular collapse, or multi-organ failure requiring emergency management
Hypertensive surges during anaesthesia, surgery, or procedures in an unprepared patient
Inadvertent beta-blockade before alpha-blockade precipitating unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and hypertensive emergency
Signs of metastatic disease or rapid tumour progression
reference.prognosis: Complete surgical removal of a benign tumour is usually curative with resolution of catecholamine excess, but hypertension may persist in some; metastatic disease carries a more guarded prognosis, and hereditary cases require indefinite surveillance for recurrence and new tumours.
pitfalls: Administering a beta-blocker before adequate alpha-blockade, risking a hypertensive crisis
Performing biopsy of an unprepared catecholamine-secreting mass
Relying on a single normal test in a strongly suspicious clinical setting
Failing to arrange genetic testing and family screening
Assuming cure without long-term biochemical follow-up given unpredictable malignant behaviour
management: Complete surgical resection (laparoscopic adrenalectomy or excision of extra-adrenal paraganglioma) is the definitive curative treatment
Preoperative preparation with alpha-adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) first, adding beta-blockade only after adequate alpha-blockade to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction
Liberalise salt and fluid intake preoperatively to counter catecholamine-induced volume contraction and prevent post-resection hypotension
Manage hypertensive crises with intravenous phentolamine or sodium nitroprusside, and never give a beta-blocker before alpha-blockade
Treat unresectable or metastatic disease with radiolabelled MIBG therapy, combination chemotherapy, somatostatin analogues or tyrosine kinase inhibitors
Lifelong biochemical surveillance with plasma or urinary fractionated metanephrines for recurrence and metachronous tumours
Offer germline genetic testing (RET, VHL, NF1, SDHx) with cascade screening and syndrome-specific surveillance of at-risk relatives
Coordinate care across endocrinology, endocrine surgery and specialist anaesthesia, and assess for catecholamine cardiomyopathy
